blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Name the measures of fiscal policy, trace an expansionary and a contractionary stance through the economy, and work out how each measure moves the budget balance.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Three levers
blocks.text: The measures are changes in the level of government spending, changes in the rates and structure of taxation, and changes in the amount the government borrows. They are set together in the yearly budget: revenue is forecast, spending is planned, and the borrowing is whatever bridges the gap between them. No lever moves alone for long - a spending rise must be financed from revenue, from borrowing, or not at all.

blocks.heading: The expansionary stance
blocks.text: An expansionary stance raises spending or cuts taxes to lift total spending in the economy. Trace it through an invented project: public money committed to the Otavi water scheme lets contracts to builders who hire where workers are idle - and where there is spare capacity, the extra spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices; near full capacity it tends instead to push prices up. The chain runs from the budget line, to the contractor, to the pay packet, to the town's shops.

blocks.heading: The contractionary stance
blocks.text: A contractionary stance cuts spending or raises taxes to slow total spending in the economy. Trace it: a frozen public wage bill and a higher vehicle duty leave households and firms with less to spend, so buying across the economy tends to cool, easing the pressure on prices - at the cost of weaker sales for firms and, in time, fewer hours of work on offer.

blocks.heading: How fiscal measures move the budget balance
blocks.text: Every fiscal measure moves the budget balance, because the balance is revenue minus spending. Other things being equal, a rise in government spending or a cut in tax rates widens a deficit or shrinks a surplus; a cut in spending or a rise in tax rates narrows a deficit or moves the budget towards surplus. Work an invented budget through. A government starts with a balanced budget: N$70 billion of revenue and N$70 billion of spending. It raises spending on school building by N$3 billion, so spending becomes 70 + 3 = 73, N$73 billion, and it cuts income tax rates, so revenue falls by N$2 billion to 70 - 2 = 68, N$68 billion. The budget now shows a deficit of 73 - 68 = 5, N$5 billion, which tends to be borrowed. Had it instead raised value-added tax to collect N$3 billion more while holding spending at N$70 billion, the result would have been a surplus of N$3 billion. The state of the economy moves the balance too, even with no change in policy. In a downturn, incomes, spending and profits fall, so tax revenue falls, while more people need support, so spending rises: the deficit widens on its own. In a boom the reverse tends to happen. During the world financial crisis of 2008 and 2009 the United Kingdom's budget deficit widened sharply, partly for this reason, as tax receipts fell and support payments rose. Measures also feed back on the balance: where a tax cut raises spending and incomes, part of the lost revenue may return through sales and income taxes, so the deficit may widen by less than the first calculation suggests.

blocks.heading: Reading a stance off a budget
blocks.text: A budget that raises spending on bridge repairs when work is scarce is expansionary; one that trims the public wage bill while prices climb is contractionary. The stance is read off what the budget does with its three levers, not off what the finance minister says about it - and a budget may be expansionary on spending while contractionary on tax, which is why the levers are read together.
